quotes.text: According to Saint Etienne's official website, the album is about "how music affects your life. How it defines the way you see the world as a child, how it can get you through bad times in unexpected ways, and how songs you've known all your life can suddenly develop a new attachment, and hurt every time you hear them. More than how it affects and reflects your life though, the album is about believing in music, living your life by its rules."

The album opens with "Over the Border", a semi-spoken memoir that narrates a first-person coming-of-age tale that is defined by musical milestones, and includes references to the likes of Peter Gabriel, Genesis, Modern English, New Order, Marc Bolan, Top of the Pops, Smash Hits, NME, Factory Records and Postcard Records.

The second track "I've Got Your Music" blends "pristine dance-pop keyboards" and "driving electro beats" with Cracknell's "smooth, cool coos", while referencing Donna Summer's 1977 song "I Feel Love".
"Heading for the Fair", the album's third track, was compared to "the kind of Balearic dance track Boys' Own Records put out in the early 90s".
"Last Days of Disco", a downbeat R&B song featuring symphonic string sections and a "lovely mellifluous" chorus.
"Tonight", the fifth track, incorporates "atmospheric" strings, "butterflies-in-your-stomach" synths and "stuttering" beats.
The sixth track, "Answer Song", was referred to as "a waltzing ballad of epically soulful proportions".
"Record Doctor", an a cappella song that pays tribute to "a friend blessed with the uncanny ability to find the right song to fit your mood".
"Popular" combines "radio-friendly electronics" and Cracknell's "sweet pop-soul vocals", with the lyrics namechecking several UK chart-topping titles.
"DJ" "starts out on the High Street but ends up in the underground club, mixing posh sounding effects and an adrenaline rush of techno synths to play out the song's conceit."
The eleventh track "When I Was Seventeen" is a 1980s rock-inspired number.
"Haunted Jukebox" sports a "mid-'60s soul groove" and "lushly lovely backing vocals", with the song's melody and vocal arrangement perceived by critics as a homage to the Carpenters.
"Haunted Jukebox" describes "a blossoming teenage romance built upon a mutual love of records", while noting "how the memories evoked by old music hit harder as you age".
Saint Etienne were perennial specialists at invoking precisely this sort of wistful reminiscence via the medium of song.

They are still charming and seducing us with new releases that merely re-assert their standing as one of our most singularly adventurous – and at the same time underrated and unsung – national treasures.

Throughout these 30-odd years of eclectic and diverse singles, albums and soundtracks that somehow transcended any kind of lazy pigeonholing or stylistic box-ticking, they have always remained true to their own maxim of what makes an expertly-crafted pop record.

Taking their cues from myriad influences, they have been steadfastly resolute in never making the same album twice. Their sheer enthusiasm and restless quest for exploring new sounds, textures, approaches and recording processes have seen them glide effortlessly across more than a dozen albums.
They have an almost encyclopedic and fanatical dedication to honing meticulously conceived records that always bring joy.
It would thus be churlish to accuse Saint Etienne of ever playing safe and releasing the same record over and over again. The simple truth is, they never have done.

Whenever they have delivered a new album, it's been either a progression or a deft distillation of whatever has been on their own perceptive radars and where their individual mindsets have been at any particular point in time. They would simply pursue their own methodology and not be overly influenced by any outside distractions – preferring an almost hermetic, even alchemic, approach to songwriting.

It was conceived and recorded remotely with the band separated across three locations, as a result of the post-Covid lockdowns. As a result, it sounds almost eerily prescient and suitably discombobulating, but no less fascinating and alluring for that reason alone.

Built almost wholly on samples of sound sources taken largely from songs of the 1990s, it presented itself as a suite of downtempo tracks whose rose-tinted nostalgia – complete with disembodied refrains – resonated perfectly with the overall strangeness that we were all experiencing during that most challenging of periods.
The fact that the music sounded exactly like snatches of [day]dream / sleepwalking sequences filtering through a semi-conscious torpor merely added to its woozy and somnambulant allure.

The band emerged in the early '90s with a club-friendly cover of Neil Young's "Only Love Can Break Your Heart," but to call it a dance-pop act would be a disservice to the astonishing body of work it's have amassed during the last 35 years. Yes, many Etienne hits rely on synthetic beats and a certain European, late-night summer glamour, but its mystique is equally informed by the pervasive nostalgia of Burt Bacharach and the cosmopolitan coolness of the '60s soundtracks by John Barry and Lalo Schifrin.
On 1998's "Good Humor," helmed by the Cardigans producer Tore Johansson, the dreamy "Mr. Donut" sounded like a cross between the Beach Boys and Dusty Springfield.
The band's haunting tribute to the Carpenters, "Downey CA," appeared on 2000's "Sound of Water" — an icy, melancholy confection, possibly the most fully realized album of its career.

And its fastidious standards of excellence have never wavered. "Home Counties," from 2017, included "Whyteleafe," a syncretic gem of harpsichord-fueled baroque, electro bass lines and vocals that both cherish and re-create the delights of vintage British pop.
Last year's radical "The Night" delved into an angelic strand of beatless ambient.

"If you're true to yourself, your musical influences are going to come out directly in your songwriting or production work," says Stanley. "The compilations are mostly things that we love, and it's like a world that you can get into."

Few bands have celebrated the concept of a B-side as an excuse to explore all sorts of oblique ideas and atmospheric impressions with the glee of Saint Etienne. Its output in that respect is monumental, and the group has produced almost as many experimental sketches as regular album tracks.

Growing up in the '80s, there were a lot of British bands like China Crisis or the Teardrop Explodes that had a massive hit, but on the B-side did more experimental stuff. That's what you can do on a B-side; you can exercise your more weird muscles.
If you ever wondered what it might sound like to hear the members of Saint Etienne djing, well here's your chance.

The Trip is a 2 cd set chock full of gems dug up from the vaults of Universal and is another excellent entry in this series (which also has compilations by Dirty Vegas, Tom Middleton, and Tim Love Lee).

Those of us who like the slinky rhythms of Serge Gainsbourg, the soulful sides of Motown, the breezy soft pop, and psychedelic 60s will revel in this sweet mix cd - and it's all mixed together with those soundbites Saint Etienne have sprinkled on their own albums.
